title: 9-Year-Old's Minecraft Videos Cost Dad $100K and His Job
summary: A 9-year-old boy named Mike loves Minecraft. He started a YouTube channel called "Mighty Mike Plays." But his videos weren't getting many views. So his dad, Dave, helped him set up a small ad campaign — just $20. But then Mike went back to YouTube's ad system on his own. He kept buying ads. The total bill? $118,000! The ads worked — Mike's videos jumped from a few hundred views to tens of thousands. But the money came from Dave's corporate credit card. When his bosses found out, Dave lost his job. Now he has about a month to pay back the money, or he might lose his house. Dave posted a video about what happened. It got over 3 million views. Some people feel bad for him. Others are skeptical. A popular YouTuber named MoistCr1tikal thinks it might be a scam. He noticed Dave is selling T-shirts instead of asking for donations. Dave says he's not trying to guilt anyone. "I genuinely have no idea what our lives are going to look like a month from now," he said. This isn't the first time kids have run up huge bills online. Many games and apps make it easy to spend money without parents knowing. Experts say parents should keep an eye on their kids' online accounts.
why_it_matters: It's a reminder that apps and websites can spend real money with just a few taps, so families should talk about money rules and watch online accounts together.

background_read: Minecraft (a video game where players build things out of blocks and explore) is one of the most popular games in the world.
YouTube (a website where people upload and watch videos) lets creators pay to show their videos to more people, and the costs add up automatically, so a bill can grow fast.
MoistCr1tikal (a popular YouTuber who reacts to strange stories on the internet) is one of the people who questioned the story, which shows how quickly an online story can spread.
Article_Structure: WHO: Mike, a 9-year-old YouTuber, his dad Dave, millions of viewers, and the YouTuber MoistCr1tikal.
WHAT: Mike bought $118,000 worth of ads for his channel, and Dave lost his job because the money came from his corporate credit card.
WHERE: On YouTube, using the site's ad system and Dave's work credit card.
WHY: It shows how easy it is for kids to spend huge amounts of money online — and how fast an internet story can spread.

perspectives.perspective: People who feel sorry for Dave
perspectives.description: They think a dad was just trying to help his son's hobby and is now in serious trouble, with only about a month to pay the money back.
They doubt the story is completely honest, because Dave is selling T-shirts instead of simply asking for donations.
They say the lesson is bigger than one family: games and apps make spending too easy, so parents should keep a close eye on their kids' online accounts.
